Where your driving habits lead.

These are the kilometres you drive right now per day, week and month. Polaris looks at your whole lease and gives more weight to the last 30 days, so a change in your habits shows here within a few weeks.

Compare it with “From now on”: if this card is higher, you are on course to go over your allowance.

What you can still drive.

These are the kilometres per day, week and month that use up your allowance exactly at the end of the lease: the kilometres you have left, spread over the time you have left.

They go up when you drive less and down when you drive more. Stay at or below them and you will not pay for extra kilometres.

Your allowance, spread evenly.

These are the kilometres per day, week and month your contract allows on average, from the first day of the lease to the last. They never change, whatever you drive.

Use them as the yardstick for the other two cards.

Did you stay within your budget?

Your budget is the distance per day that brings you exactly to your allowance at the end of the lease.

Each row is a period: today (since midnight), then the last 7, 14 and 30 days.
They all end at your latest reading.

Under each period, two figures:
• what you drove
• what the budget allowed
For example “320 / 280 km”: you drove 320 km where the budget allowed 280.

The gap on the right says by how much:
• red with a +, you drove more than allowed
• green with a −, less
The percentage gives this gap against the second figure.

Polaris uses the budget as it was at the start of the period, recorded every day at midnight.

The “Live” badge on the first row: the snapshot of today is not saved yet, because Polaris saves it at midnight. The row is then compared with a projection rebuilt just now. These live figures are what the midnight job would have saved; nothing is stored from them.

If even that is not possible, the row is compared with the latest earlier record and says “Since yesterday” or “Since N days ago”.

Are you driving more or less than usual?

Your usual pace is your average distance per day since the start of the lease, with more weight on the last 30 days.

Each row is a period: today (since midnight), then the last 7, 14 and 30 days.
They all end at your latest reading.

Under each period, two figures:
• what you drove
• what your pace predicted
For example “320 / 280 km”: you drove 40 km more than usual.

The gap on the right says by how much:
• red with a +, you drove more than usual
• green with a −, less
The percentage gives this gap against the second figure.

Polaris records your pace every day at midnight.
Until it has a record for the first day of a period, the row says “Not enough history”.

The “Live” badge on the first row: the snapshot of today is not saved yet, because Polaris saves it at midnight. The row is then compared with a projection rebuilt just now. These live figures are what the midnight job would have saved; nothing is stored from them.

If even that is not possible, the row is compared with the latest earlier record and says “Since yesterday” or “Since N days ago”.

Is your end of lease looking better or worse?

Every day, Polaris estimates how far you will have driven by the end of the lease. This panel compares today’s estimate with the one from the start of each period.

Each row is a period: today (since midnight), then the last 7, 14 and 30 days.
They all end at your latest reading.

Under each period, two figures:
• today’s estimate
• the estimate Polaris made at the start of the period
For example “61,200 / 60,500 km”: your estimate went up by 700 km since the start of the period.

The gap on the right says by how much:
• red with a +, the estimate went up
• green with a −, it went down: you are driving less than before
The percentage gives this gap against the second figure.

Polaris records its estimate every day at midnight.
Until it has a record for the first day of a period, the row says “Not enough history”.

The “Live” badge on the first row: the snapshot of today is not saved yet, because Polaris saves it at midnight. The row is then compared with a projection rebuilt just now. These live figures are what the midnight job would have saved; nothing is stored from them.

If even that is not possible, the row is compared with the latest earlier record and says “Since yesterday” or “Since N days ago”.
